0.body: ZombieNet SDK is a Rust testing framework for Polkadot SDK -based blockchains. It spawns ephemeral blockchain networks programmatically for testing and development. The SDK succeeds the original ZombieNet (TypeScript), offering a type-safe, composable Rust API. Migrating from TypeScript ZombieNet? The TOML configuration format is largely compatible. See Network Definition Spec for the full reference.
0.title: Introduction

1.body: Programmatic Network Spawning - Define and spawn relay chains and parachains from Rust code Fluent Builder API - Compose networks using a chainable builder pattern Multiple Providers - Run on Kubernetes, Podman, Docker, or natively Metrics & Assertions - Query Prometheus metrics and validate network behavior Subxt Integration - Interact with networks using subxt

13.body: This document covers the two core aspects of what ZombieNet does under the hood: chain spec customization and command-line argument generation .
13.breadcrumbs: How It Works » How It Works
13.title: How It Works

14.body: When spawning a network, ZombieNet modifies chain specifications to configure the test environment. These customizations happen automatically based on your network configuration.
14.breadcrumbs: How It Works » Chain Spec Customization
14.title: Chain Spec Customization

15.body: The framework applies these modifications to relay chain specs: Customization Description Runtime Genesis Patch Merges user-provided genesis_overrides JSON (applied first): objects merge, any other value replaces Genesis Patch Applies the genesis_patch RFC 6902 operations after the overrides; add at /- appends to a list. Needs a plain chain spec. A replace path, or the parent of an add path, must exist once genesis is merged. The steps below run after the patch, so what they rewrite (authorities, stakers, invulnerables, validatorCount, node balances) wins over it Clear Authorities Removes existing authorities from session/keys, aura/authorities, grandpa/authorities, collatorSelection/invulnerables, and staking/invulnerables + staking/stakers (relay only). Also sets validatorCount to 0 unless devStakers is configured. Add Balances Adds balances for each node's sr and sr_stash accounts. Balance is max(initial_balance, staking_min * 2). Only nodes with initial_balance > 0 receive balances. Add Zombie Account Adds //Zombie account with 1000 units (in chain denomination, i.e., 1000 * 10^token_decimals planck) for internal operations Add Staking Configures staking for validators with minimum stake Add Session Authorities Adds validators as session authorities (if session pallet exists) Add Aura/Grandpa Authorities For chains without session pallet Add HRMP Channels Configures cross-chain messaging channels Register Parachains Adds InGenesis parachains to genesis
15.breadcrumbs: How It Works » Relay Chain Customizations
15.title: Relay Chain Customizations

16.body: For cumulus-based parachains: Customization Description Override para_id/paraId Sets correct parachain ID in chain spec root (both para_id and paraId variants) Override relay_chain Sets relay chain ID in chain spec root Apply Genesis Overrides Merges user-provided JSON overrides Genesis Patch Applies the genesis_patch RFC 6902 operations after the overrides, before the authorities and balances below are rewritten Clear/Add Authorities Clears existing authorities from session/keys, aura/authorities, grandpa/authorities, collatorSelection/invulnerables. Then adds collator session keys (if session pallet exists) or aura authorities. Add Collator Selection Adds invulnerable collators to collatorSelection/invulnerables Override parachainInfo Sets correct parachainId in /parachainInfo/parachainId Add Balances Extracts accounts from assets pallet metadata and ensures they have native token balances. Adds balances for collator sr accounts. For EVM-based parachains (is_evm_based = true), Ethereum session keys are generated and used instead of standard keys.
16.title: Parachain Customizations

17.body:
ZombieNet supports customizing session key types and their cryptographic schemes via the chain_spec_key_types configuration option. Cryptographic Schemes Scheme Suffix Description SR25519 _sr Schnorr signatures, used by most runtime keys ED25519 _ed Edwards curve signatures, used by grandpa ECDSA _ec Elliptic curve, used by beefy and Ethereum compatibility Predefined Key Types These key types have predefined default schemes: Key Type Default Scheme Notes aura SR25519 ED25519 on asset-hub-polkadot babe SR25519 grandpa ED25519 beefy ECDSA im_online SR25519 authority_discovery SR25519 para_validator SR25519 para_assignment SR25519 parachain_validator SR25519 nimbus SR25519 vrf SR25519 Syntax Two formats are supported: Short form : aura — uses the predefined default scheme Long form : aura_ed — explicitly specifies the scheme Unknown key types default to SR25519 when using short form. Example [relaychain]
chain_spec_key_types = ["aura", "grandpa", "beefy"] # Uses defaults # Or with explicit schemes:
chain_spec_key_types = ["aura_ed", "grandpa_sr", "custom_key_ec"]
17.breadcrumbs: How It Works » Chain Spec Key Types
17.title: Chain Spec Key Types

20.body: These arguments are always set by the framework and filtered out if provided by user configuration: Argument Value --chain Generated chain spec path --name Node name from config --rpc-cors all --rpc-methods unsafe --parachain-id Parachain ID (relay chain nodes only, when para_id is specified; NOT used for cumulus collators) --node-key Deterministic key derived from node name Additionally, these flags are managed by the framework: Flag When Added --no-telemetry Relay chain nodes only (not cumulus collators) --collator Cumulus collators with is_validator: true --execution wasm Embedded relay chain full node (after -- separator)
20.title: Framework-Managed Arguments

21.body: Argument Condition --validator Relay chain nodes with is_validator: true --insecure-validator-i-know-what-i-do Validators, if the binary supports it --prometheus-external Unless already in user args --unsafe-rpc-external Only for Docker/Kubernetes providers (not native) --bootnodes When bootnode addresses are available
21.breadcrumbs: How It Works » Arguments Added Conditionally
21.title: Arguments Added Conditionally

22.body: The framework injects port arguments based on assigned ports: Argument Description --prometheus-port Prometheus metrics port --rpc-port RPC/WebSocket port --listen-addr P2P listen address (format: /ip4/0.0.0.0/tcp/{port}/ws) --base-path Data directory path
22.title: Port Arguments

23.body: Cumulus-based collators receive two sets of arguments separated by --: Before -- (collator arguments): --chain (parachain spec) --collator --prometheus-port, --rpc-port, --listen-addr --base-path User-provided collator args After -- (embedded relay chain full node): --base-path (separate relay data directory) --chain (relay chain spec) --execution wasm (hardcoded, always WASM execution) --port (full node P2P port, injected by framework when assigned port differs from default 30333) --prometheus-port (full node metrics port, injected by framework when assigned port differs from default 9616) User-provided full node args
23.breadcrumbs: How It Works » Cumulus Collator Arguments
23.title: Cumulus Collator Arguments

24.body:
Use the -: prefix to remove arguments that the framework adds: [[relaychain.nodes]]
name = "bob"
args = ["-:--insecure-validator-i-know-what-i-do"] This removes --insecure-validator-i-know-what-i-do from bob's command line. The removal syntax: -:--flag-name removes --flag-name -:flag-name also removes --flag-name (normalized automatically) Works for both flags and options (the option's value is also removed)

45.body: By default zombienet builds the JIP-4 chain spec itself, with jam-chainspec . The genesis is the same one the node's gen-spec writes: the network's validators, the bootstrap service as service 0 (hosting the null authorizer) and the null authorizer on every core. The bootstrap service comes from [jamchain.genesis] bootstrap_service (a path or a url), or is embedded in zombienet with the jam feature (of zombienet-sdk, zombienet-orchestrator or the CLI), so no extra file is needed: zombienet-sdk = { version = "...", features = ["jam"] } The feature builds it from the jam-bootstrap-service crate when zombienet is compiled, which needs the rust-src component (rustup component add rust-src); it is off by default so other users don't need it. To embed a prebuilt blob instead, set ZOMBIE_JAM_BOOTSTRAP_SERVICE_BLOB to its path when building with the feature. Without the feature and without bootstrap_service, building the spec fails and says so (unless with_defaults = false). The built-in builder needs exactly as many validator nodes as the protocol parameters call for (6 for tiny, 78 for mini, 1023 for full). How the spec is produced: Set Spec chain_spec_path Used as given (a path or a url). chain_spec_command or genesis_overrides Generated with <command> gen-spec <config> <spec>, from the jam_config.json zombienet writes. nothing (default) Built in process, customized by [jamchain.genesis]. genesis can't be combined with the other three, nor chain_spec_path with the generator fields.

46.body:
[jamchain.genesis]
# Replace the embedded bootstrap service with another blob (a path or a url).
# bootstrap_service = "./blobs/jam-bootstrap-service.jam"
# Don't add the bootstrap service nor the null authorizer queues.
# with_defaults = false
# A native jam-chainspec JSON config, layered under the fields below. Its `id`,
# `genesis_validators` and `protocol_parameters` are replaced by zombienet's.
# config_file = "./my-chainspec-config.json"
# A full protocol parameters object, instead of the `protocol_params_type` preset.
# protocol_parameters = { ... } [jamchain.genesis.services.5]
code = "./blobs/my-service.jam" # a path or a url
balance = "min+1000000" # 1000 | "max" | "min" | "min+<amount>"
min_item_gas = 10
min_memo_gas = 10
deposit_offset = 0 # an amount, or "max"
preimages = ["./blobs/my-authorizer.jam"]
storage = { "0x6772656574696e67" = "0x68656c6c6f" } [jamchain.genesis.auth_queues]
0 = [{ code = "./blobs/my-authorizer.jam", config = "0x" }] # hashed by zombienet
1 = ["null"] # or a 0x-prefixed hash [jamchain.genesis.privileges]
manager = 0 # alias: bless
delegator = 0 # alias: designate
registrar = 0 # alias: register
assign = { 0 = 5 }
always_acc = { 5 = 1000000 } Relative paths are resolved against the network definition's directory. Balances that don't fit a TOML integer (like u64::MAX) are written as strings, or as "max". use zombienet_sdk::{jam::JamAuthorizer, NetworkConfigBuilder}; let config = NetworkConfigBuilder::new() .with_jamchain(|j| { j.with_id("dev") .with_genesis(|g| { g.with_service(5, |s| { s.with_code("./blobs/my-service.jam") .with_balance(zombienet_sdk::jam::JamBalance::MinimumPlus(1_000_000)) .with_preimage("./blobs/my-authorizer.jam") .with_storage(b"greeting".to_vec(), b"hello".to_vec()) }) .with_auth_queue(0, [JamAuthorizer::code("./blobs/my-authorizer.jam")]) .with_auth_queue(1, [JamAuthorizer::Null]) .with_assigner([0], 5) // .with_bootstrap_service("https://example.com/jam-bootstrap-service.jam") }) .with_validator(|n| n.with_name("jam0")) // ... 6 validators for tiny }) .build() .unwrap(); The network's base directory gets jam_spec.json and, for a spec built in process, jam_genesis.json: the genesis that went into it, with the code hash of every service and where the bootstrap service came from. The bootstrap service must suit the node: the embedded one is built from the jam-bootstrap-service version matching the jam-* crates zombienet uses. For a node on another version, point bootstrap_service at its blob, or generate the spec with chain_spec_command = "polkajam". The protocol parameters are process-wide, so all the JAM networks a process builds in process must use the same set. The SDK also exports the embedded blobs for tests: zombienet_sdk::jam::NULL_AUTHORIZER_BLOB, null_authorizer_hash(), embedded_bootstrap_service() and, with the jam feature, BOOTSTRAP_SERVICE_BLOB, BOOTSTRAP_SERVICE_HASH and BOOTSTRAP_SERVICE_SOURCE.

60.body: Allow to set custom processes to spawn after the network is up: services that run next to the nodes, such as an RPC adapter, an IPFS daemon or a database another process needs. A custom process is a member of the network like a node: it is tracked on the Network, written to zombie.json, attached to again from it and destroyed with the namespace. Look it up with network.get_custom_process("name") or list them with network.custom_processes(). A process may not share its name with a node, since they share one registry: in TOML the process is rejected; in the builder a node declared after a process with its name is renamed, as it would be after another node, so declare processes last. Unlike nodes, a custom process runs its command directly, not through zombienet's wrapper script: most of them are off-the-shelf images, which may not have bash. On docker and kubernetes the pause/resume/restart controls go through that wrapper, so on a custom process they return an error; on native they signal the process and work as for nodes. A process must listen on all interfaces (0.0.0.0) on docker and kubernetes, where it is reached through a published port or a Service; one bound to 127.0.0.1 is reachable from nowhere. Most daemons need a flag for that (--rpc-external for eth-rpc below, --host 0.0.0.0 and the like elsewhere). A process gets the same writable /data directory a node gets, on every provider; that is where kubo above keeps its repo (IPFS_PATH) and where anything that must survive a restart of the process belongs. command replaces the image's entrypoint , on every provider. An image whose entrypoint does setup work (kubo's runs ipfs init and binds the API and gateway to all interfaces; the postgres image's runs initdb) needs that entrypoint named as the command, with the image's usual arguments as args.

63.body: The args and env values of a process may refer to the nodes, which are all running by then, with the same {{ZOMBIE:<node-name>:<field>}} placeholders node args use: ws_uri, internal_ws_uri (the address other members of the network use, which is what a process wants), multiaddr, prometheus_uri for a substrate node, rpc_uri and peer_addr for a JAM node. On docker a node's addresses are host addresses, so a process in a container reaches a node only through the host (host.docker.internal on Docker Desktop). They may also refer to any custom process's ports, their own or another's, as {{ZOMBIE:<process-name>:port_<port-name>}}, since every port is picked before anything starts (see Lifecycle). A placeholder that resolves to nothing (a node or port that does not exist) means the process is never started, which fails the spawn (see Lifecycle).

65.body:
A process is ready when its ready_check passes: tcp = "<port name>", the port accepts a connection, or http = { port = "<port name>", path = "/health" }, a GET answers 2xx, every interval seconds (1 by default). The process's timeout, in seconds, bounds the wait (the global node_spawn_timeout by default); a one-shot is waited on to exit within it, and has failed when it does not. Without a check, a process with ports is ready when its first port accepts a TCP connection, and one without ports is ready once started. On kubernetes the check is the pod's readiness probe, so the kubelet does the checking from inside the cluster and the Service routes only once it passes; on docker and native zombienet probes from where it runs. On docker a published port answers for docker's proxy whether or not the process listens, so a tcp check there, including the default on the first port, passes at once and gives no real ordering; zombienet warns about it at spawn, and http is the check to use there. A one-shot process (one_shot = true) runs to completion within its timeout: exit 0 is success, anything else a failure. It has no readiness, so no ready_check. On kubernetes a custom process's pod is never restarted by the kubelet, one-shot or not: a process that exits is done, by success or by failure, and its pod says so. depends_on lists the processes this one starts after, with a condition as docker-compose names them: service_started, service_healthy (passed its check), service_completed_successfully (a one-shot that exited 0). A bare name means the target's natural condition: completed for a one-shot, healthy when it has a check or a port, started otherwise. Every process starts as soon as its dependencies are met, in parallel with whatever else can start; one with no dependencies starts once the nodes are up. A dependency must name a custom process, its condition must fit the target, and there may be no cycle; all three are checked when the config loads. [[custom_processes]]
name = "migrate"
image = "docker.io/library/postgres:16"
command = "psql"
args = [ "-h", "db", "-f", "/data/schema.sql" ]
one_shot = true
depends_on = ["db"] [[custom_processes]]
name = "api"
image = "example/api:1.0"
command = "api"
ports = [ { name = "http", port = 8080 } ]
ready_check = { http = { port = "http", path = "/health" } }
timeout = 120
depends_on = [ "migrate", { name = "cache", condition = "service_started" } ] Every process is required: one that does not meet its condition within its timeout, or is never started (its ports could not be reserved, a dependency did not meet its condition, a placeholder did not resolve), fails the spawn , as a node that never comes up does; the error names the process and the reason, and the network is cleaned up when its provider is dropped (on native the logs stay in base_dir). On a spawned network process.state() is Ready or Completed, written to zombie.json. wait_ready() on a process waits for its condition again and reports Failed { reason } when it is no longer met; the network-wide wait_until_is_up() leaves processes out. Processes start at most spawn_concurrency at a time, the value as set, where nodes drop to one at a time whenever a node or chain spec has {{ZOMBIE:..}} placeholders. Placeholders in a process do not limit the nodes. A process may name another's port the way it names its own, {{ZOMBIE:<process>:port_<name>}}, since every port is picked before anything starts. The host part of the address is the other process's name on kubernetes and the host itself on native; on docker the containers have no names for each other, so the placeholder is of little use there.

65.title: Lifecycle

66.body:
injected_files puts files in place before the process starts, the way a node gets its chain spec: local_path on the host running zombienet (a path starting with . is resolved against the TOML's directory, as command is), remote_path where the process reads it, an absolute path to a file, unique within the process and written plainly (no ., .. or //), not inside another injected file's path and not one of the directories every process gets (/cfg, /data, /relay-data) nor under /scripts or /helpers, which the containers share, mode its permissions in octal (0644 unless set, at most 0777). A local file that is not there is rejected before anything spawns. On docker and kubernetes a parent directory that is not in the image is created for the mount, owned by root, so a file goes next to what a non-root process writes, not inside it. [[custom_processes]]
name = "migrate"
image = "docker.io/library/postgres:16"
command = "psql"
args = [ "-h", "db", "-f", "/schema/init.sql" ]
one_shot = true
injected_files = [ { local_path = "./sql/init.sql", remote_path = "/schema/init.sql" } ] On docker each file is bind-mounted into the container and on kubernetes an init container fetches the files from the network's fileserver into a volume the container mounts them from, read-only in both cases, so they are in place before the container starts whatever the image is. On native the file is copied under the process's own directory in base_dir, read-only as well, and its remote_path wherever it stands in command, args and env becomes that full path, so the one config works on every provider and a command may be an injected script.
66.breadcrumbs: Network Definition Spec » Custom Processes » Injected files
66.title: Injected files

67.body:
On kubernetes an env value may come from a Secret in the namespace instead of the config: { name = "TURN_SECRET", secret = { name = "turn", key = "secret" } } sets TURN_SECRET to the secret key of the Secret turn, as a pod's valueFrom.secretKeyRef does, so a credential never passes through the TOML or zombienet. The Secret has to be in the namespace, with that key, when the process is spawned, or the spawn fails naming both; where zombienet itself may not read Secrets that check is skipped with a warning and a missing one shows as the process timing out. A namespace zombienet creates is new, so the Secret goes in one created beforehand and the network is spawned into it with spawn_k8s_in_namespace; destroy then deletes that namespace, Secret included. zombie-cli always creates its namespace, so from the CLI there is no Secret to read. A config with such an entry is rejected on native and docker before anything spawns. [[custom_processes]]
name = "api"
image = "example/api:1.0"
command = "api"
env = [ { name = "RUST_LOG", value = "info" }, { name = "TURN_SECRET", secret = { name = "turn", key = "secret" } },
]

97.body: Option Short Default Description --provider -p docker Provider: native, docker, or k8s --dir -d Random temp Base directory for network files --spawn-concurrency -c 20 Concurrent node spawn processes --node-verifier -v metric Readiness check: metric or none
97.title: Options

98.body:

zombie-cli spawn network.toml --provider native # Spawn with custom directory
zombie-cli spawn network.toml --dir /tmp/my-network # Spawn with Docker (default)
zombie-cli spawn network.toml # Spawn on Kubernetes
zombie-cli spawn network.toml --provider k8s
